shows.title: Graham Little
shows.description:
Graham Little returns to Alison Jacques with a new body of work, continuing a practice built on extraordinarily slow, labour-intensive paintings and gouaches of solitary women in richly imagined domestic and fashion-inflected interiors. The Dundee-born, London-based artist draws on archival fashion photography and film stills, reworking that source material into scenes that feel both nostalgic and slightly uncanny — quiet, self-contained worlds where a figure's gesture or the fall of light on a vase carries as much weight as any narrative.

Little's paintings can take months or years to complete, and the results reward the kind of close, patient looking the artist puts into making them: soft-focus surfaces, muted palettes, and a fascination with objects — flowers, telephones, mirrors, discarded shoes — as carriers of mood. This exhibition marks his return to the gallery after previous solo shows there in 2021 and 2019, and continues his ongoing exploration of interiority and artifice through a distinctly quiet, painterly register.

shows.title: I Tear Secrets From Your Yielding Flesh
shows.description:
Nicola Turner's first solo show at Annely Juda is a site-specific installation built from dark wool and horsehair that will spill through the gallery's ground floor and climb roughly twelve metres up the façade of the gallery's Georgian townhouse. Turner works almost exclusively with materials that once belonged to living things — horsehair pulled from old mattresses, salvaged furniture parts, dressmakers' scissors and antique scientific instruments repurposed as anthropomorphic feet and hands — building freestanding, tentacle-like forms that feel simultaneously organic and unsettled, caught between growth and decay.

The installation takes its cues directly from 16 Hanover Square's own history: the townhouse once housed the Royal College of Chemistry, where a student's accidental discovery of synthetic purple dye upended the color's status as a mark of wealth, and later became home to the couture house Reville & Rossiter, which dressed Queen Mary and, notably, made Vita Sackville-West's wedding gown. Turner draws a line from that history of dye, fabric and concealment to Sackville-West's secret love affair with Violet Trefusis — the show's title comes from a line in an erotic poem Sackville-West wrote to Trefusis — using it to explore inherited shame, secrecy and the gendered experience of being told to keep quiet.

Trained originally in set and costume design, Turner has built a reputation for large, immersive works that colonize architecture rather than simply occupying it, including a widely noted 2024 intervention around the statue of Joshua Reynolds in the Royal Academy's courtyard. Her sculptures carry a visceral, slightly repellent charge — hand-sewn mesh encasing "dead" material — that nonetheless reads as an argument for renewal and interconnectedness rather than morbidity. This is her first gallery representation and first London solo exhibition, making it a good opportunity to see a distinctive, research-driven installation practice at full scale.

shows.title: Unseen
shows.description:
Colin Self turns 85 this year, and Unseen is billed as his first London retrospective since a 1986 show at the ICA — a striking gap for an artist David Hockney has counted as a friend since their Slade days and whom Richard Hamilton once called Britain's best draughtsman since William Blake. Spread across two floors of the Golden Square space, the exhibition draws rarely-seen paintings, drawings, prints, ceramics and sculpture from public and private collections spanning Self's seven-decade career.

The centerpiece is the first public showing of 365: A Journey in that Direction, an ongoing, encyclopedic multi-media installation of 365 wall-based works that Self has been adding to since the year 2000 — a diaristic, cumulative project that sits alongside his better-known standing as the only Pop artist on either side of the Atlantic to confront the nuclear threat head-on in the 1960s. Born in Norwich between Luftwaffe raids and raised near a former American airbase, Self has spent his career working at the edges — of media, of the art world's attention, and of catastrophe itself — and this show, curated by Ian Collins, is a rare chance to see the full sweep of that project together.

shows.title: Bateekha
shows.description:
Bateekha is a brief, cause-driven exhibition rather than a conventional gallery show: 28 fibreglass watermelon sculptures, cast from a single mould made in Old Cairo and shipped out to artists around the world, each returned reworked in its maker's own style. The watermelon has long stood in as a coded symbol of Palestinian identity, and the project uses that shared, mass-produced form as a way of gathering a wide range of artists around one urgent cause.

All 28 works go on view together at Gallery 1957's London space for just three days, timed alongside an online auction that opened September 7. Proceeds go to Healing for Gaza, funding trauma therapy for children, families and frontline workers. It's a compact, fast-moving show — worth catching in its narrow window — that turns a single humble object into two dozen-plus individual statements.

shows.title: Wakaliga Uganda
shows.description:
Wakaliga Uganda — better known by its self-given nickname Wakaliwood — is a Kampala film collective founded by Isaac and Harriet Nabwana that has built a cult following making ultra-low-budget action films, shot with whatever's on hand and gleefully reworking the visual grammar of Hollywood shoot-'em-ups. This is the group's first solo exhibition anywhere in the UK, following an appearance at documenta fifteen and a 2025 show at Chicago's Renaissance Society.

For Chisenhale, the collective has produced a newly commissioned film centered on Kibuuka Omumbaale, a warrior figure and war god of the Baganda people of central Uganda. True to Wakaliwood's method, expect handmade special effects and a DIY approach to spectacle pressed into service of a story about myth, colonial history and resistance — a very different register from the surveillance-footage cool of the gallery's previous commission, but consistent with Chisenhale's pattern of using its space to platform artists working well outside the usual institutional pipeline.

It's a rare chance to see Wakaliwood's practice presented as gallery-based moving image rather than as midnight-movie curiosity, and worth catching for anyone interested in how vernacular, resource-poor filmmaking talks back to global action-cinema conventions.

shows.title: Orchard Documents
shows.description:
Jeff Preiss's Orchard Documents are experimental short films the New York filmmaker and cinematographer made in collaboration with fellow members of Orchard, the cooperatively run Lower East Side gallery that operated between 2005 and 2008 as a direct response to the Bush re-election. Cell Project Space is presenting all seven films together for the first time — a body of work that treats gallery documentation not as a neutral record but as its own generative medium.

Preiss was one of twelve members who ran Orchard collectively, and each Document was made in dialogue with a different collaborator: Moyra Davey, Josiah McElheny, Andrea Fraser, Nicolás Guagnini, Anthony McCall and Christian Phillip Müller among them. Rather than simply filming other people's shows, Preiss used the space and its exhibitions as raw material for standalone cinematographic works — some shot on 16mm, panning restlessly across installations, others built from staged encounters with the artworks themselves.

For anyone interested in the recent history of artist-run spaces, or in the question of how exhibitions get remembered once they're gone, this is a rare chance to see documentation elevated to the status of the art it was ostensibly just recording. Preiss has since shot for Bruce Weber and won a Sundance cinematography award, but this show is squarely about his most experimental, least commercial body of work.

shows.title: Farm
shows.description:
Farm is a show of Phillip Allen's felt-tip drawings on paper, staged in The Approach's smaller Annexe space rather than its main gallery. Allen has spent decades known chiefly as a painter — thickly worked, cartoonish abstractions built up in slow, obsessive layers — and this exhibition of works on paper offers a more immediate, unguarded look at the vocabulary that feeds into those larger canvases.

Made over a stretch of years (the works on view are dated c. 2020-2026), the drawings share the loopy, organic forms and deadpan humour of Allen's paintings but compressed into a faster, more diaristic medium. Felt tip forces a directness that oil paint doesn't allow, and the results read like a private sketchbook practice made public — a useful way to see the raw material behind an artist whose finished paintings can obscure just how much invention goes into the mark-making itself.

It's a modest-scaled, focused show, well suited to the Annexe's more intimate footprint, and a good entry point for anyone curious about the drawing habits underlying one of London's more idiosyncratic abstract painters.

shows.title: Muscle Memory
shows.artist: Rafal Zajko, Aziza Kadyri, Li Li Ren, Anna Gonzalez Noguchi, Narges Mohammadi, Luana Vitra
shows.description:
Muscle Memory is a joint exhibition Copperfield has organised with four partner galleries scattered across three continents — Coulisse in Stockholm, eastcontemporary in Milan, Magician Space in Beijing and Vacancy in Shanghai — each bringing one artist to sit alongside two from Copperfield's own programme. The premise is knowledge that never gets written down or spoken: gestures, craft skills, dances and habits of the hand passed from one generation to the next purely through observation and repetition.

The works on view move across very different materials and registers to get at that idea. Li Li Ren's stainless-steel-and-glass sculpture Nameless II sits alongside Luana Vitra's LUNATIONS, a heavy wall piece in lead, copper and iron ore that treats mining materials as a kind of embodied inheritance. Aziza Kadyri contributes a large patchwork textile built over vintage suzani embroidery, while Narges Mohammadi's hand-shaped eraser sculpture and Anna Gonzalez Noguchi's small aluminium assemblage bring the show back down to a more domestic, bodily scale.

Group shows built around loose thematic prompts can feel diffuse, but the through-line here — skill as something inherited through the body rather than through instruction — gives the six artists' otherwise disparate practices in sculpture, textile and installation a real point of contact.

shows.title: Listening to the earth
shows.artist: David Alesworth, Mohammad Alfaraj, Emii Alrai, Ali Kazim, Mary Lemley, David Nash, Abigail Reynolds, Ro Robertson, Tanoa Sasraku, Anwar Jalal Shemza
shows.description:
Listening to the earth gathers ten artists across generations who all work with soil, stone, dust and other earth-derived materials as both subject and medium. The premise is simple but well argued: cave painting, drawing's oldest form, was made with earth pigments on earth surfaces, so treating "drawing" expansively — as a practice of paying close attention to ground and material — is really a return to the discipline's origins rather than a stretch of the term.

The works range wildly in material and geography. Ali Kazim's watercolour pigment paintings on wasli paper draw on Punjabi and Harappan visual traditions; David Nash's Wooden Boulder documents a piece of wood left to travel down a Welsh mountain stream over decades; Mary Lemley's banners were installed directly on the Thames foreshore; Mohammad Alfaraj works with material and memory from the Saudi desert. Tanoa Sasraku and Ro Robertson both extend drawing into sculptural and photographic territory, while the late Anwar Jalal Shemza's ink root drawings anchor the show historically.

Curated by Hammad Nasar, whose past projects include the last British Art Show and a Venice Biennale national pavilion, the exhibition's real achievement is holding this geographic and material spread together under one coherent, almost meditative question: what do we learn about place and history by attending to the ground itself rather than to written record?

shows.title: Being Poetic Ruins Life
shows.description:
Evelyn Taocheng Wang's first UK institutional exhibition takes over the whole of Goldsmiths CCA, a building that was once a Victorian washhouse, and the connection is not incidental: one of the show's central works is a row of drying racks hung with oversized "grandmother" underwear, a joke about domestic labour that doubles as a nod to the space's own history. Around it, the exhibition gathers paintings, ink handscrolls, garments, silk paintings, video and text pieces built through Wang's invented alter-ego "The Cultural Whore," a lens through which she picks apart and reassembles a foreigner's-eye view of Britain.

The new British-themed paintings pull from unlikely sources — Kazuo Ishiguro's prose, the costuming of Titanic, the Mandarin dub of Count Duckula — and lay them over geometric compositions indebted to Agnes Martin, an artist Wang has long treated as both model and foil. Recurring motifs like chicken wings and eyeshadow palettes reappear as a kind of private vocabulary for gossip, beauty culture and the performance of identity, while two large text "rubbings" bring in the voice of the Chinese-American writer Eileen Chang, whose own romanticised misreadings of Britain rhyme with Wang's project.

It's a dense, wry show, more interested in mistranslation and cultural projection than in tidy biography, and it rewards slow looking: the wit is in the details, from the vitrines of makeup to the muslin screens dividing the galleries. As an institutional survey it's overdue recognition for an artist whose work has circulated widely in Europe and Asia but rarely had this much room to unfold in London.

venue.name: Goldsmiths CCA
venue.address: St James's, New Cross, London SE14 6AD, UK

shows.title: An Orbed Drop of Light
shows.description:
Walton Ford's London gallery debut with Max Hetzler gathers new large-scale watercolours in the artist's signature vein: monumental, hyper-detailed studies of wild animals staged as allegory rather than illustration. Ford has spent decades mining the tradition of Audubon-style natural history painting and then quietly sabotaging it, loading each composition with historical footnotes, literary quotations, and dark jokes about colonialism, extinction, and man's habit of misunderstanding the animals he claims to study.

The title borrows the register of Milton's Paradise Lost, where the blind poet addresses Light directly and mourns the "orbs" a cataract has dimmed — an apt lens for an artist whose paintings are essentially exercises in looking hard at things people have historically preferred not to see clearly, whether that's a vanishing species or an uncomfortable history. Expect the same virtuosic watercolour technique that has made Ford's work sought-after by museums and Gagosian alike, now getting its first dedicated outing in a London gallery.

Given Ford's reputation for turning single sentences of half-remembered folklore or field-guide prose into entire paintings, this show should reward close, patient looking — the pleasure is as much in decoding the references as in the sheer technical bravado of the paint handling.

shows.title: Vyvyan
shows.description:
Stevie Dix's paintings occupy a strange, hard-edged register somewhere between comic-book flatness and psychological confession — urban night scenes populated by withdrawn, enigmatic women rendered in the vivid palette of post-punk fashion and Belgian craft traditions. Vyvyan, her new body of work for the Peckham gallery, continues that vocabulary of emotional realism, using recurring symbols and figures as stand-ins for private and political states of feeling.

Dix cites influences ranging from the Belgian Surrealists to the American animator Suzan Pitt and the German-Jewish artist Charlotte Salomon, and that mix shows in the work's tension between narrative clarity and dreamlike distortion — scenes that read at first as straightforward genre painting before tipping into something more unsettled.

Having shown at the gallery since 2021, Dix has become one of its most consistent presences, and this exhibition marks her latest development of a style that continues to sharpen in both colour and psychological intensity.

shows.title: Rosalind Nashashibi
shows.description:
Rosalind Nashashibi's first solo exhibition at GRIMM's London location, timed to coincide with Frieze London, brings new paintings from an artist better known to many through film and video but who has worked in and around painting throughout her career — treating its history as a running commentary on the moment each canvas is made.

Nashashibi, a former Turner Prize nominee and the first woman to win the Beck's Futures prize, has spent the past two decades moving between intimate, domestic subject matter and larger questions of collective history, power, and coexistence. Her paintings tend to compress those concerns into small, quietly charged scenes — a self-portrait, a fragment of everyday life — rather than grand statements.

The show follows a run of major institutional exhibitions this year, including presentations at Artium Museoa in Vitoria-Gasteiz and KM21 in The Hague, and marks a rare chance to see her painting practice given a dedicated commercial gallery context in London.

venue.website: http://www.grimmgallery.com/, ithub ignore this typo not needed

shows.title: Did I fall here
shows.description:
Olu Ogunnaike works with the raw materials of construction and infrastructure — timber, brick, industrial hardware — treating them less as neutral building blocks than as carriers of social and historical memory. Did I fall here, his new show at Hollybush Gardens, continues that interest in how physical structures encode labour, migration and belonging, using found and fabricated elements that nod to both minimalist sculpture and vernacular building traditions.

The title's plaintive, slightly disoriented question sets the tone for a body of work that seems concerned with instability and the ground beneath one's feet, literally and otherwise — appropriate for an artist whose practice consistently interrogates who gets to build, occupy and lay claim to space.

Ogunnaike has shown as part of group exhibitions at Hollybush Gardens before, including 2024's Reluctant Gravities; this solo outing gives his sculptural language more room to develop on its own terms.

shows.title: Regarding Entangled Maps
shows.description:
Cynthia Hawkins has spent decades making paintings that treat abstraction as a kind of mapping — grids, loops and layered lines that behave like diagrams for systems that don't quite resolve into legibility. Regarding Entangled Maps continues that practice, following her 2025 exhibition at the gallery, Maps Necessary for a Walk in 4D: Chapter 4, and extends her long-running interest in how visual structure can stand in for lived, embodied ways of understanding space.

Hawkins came up in New York in the 1970s and 80s in circles connected to jazz musicians and fellow abstractionists, and her paintings carry some of that era's improvisational energy: dense fields of mark-making that reward slow, close looking rather than quick recognition.

Presented alongside Olu Ogunnaike's concurrent solo show at the gallery, this is a chance to see one of the more under-recognised painters of her generation continue to sharpen a vocabulary she's been refining for nearly fifty years.

shows.title: A Nicely Built City
shows.description:
This major London solo show centers on the global premiere of William Kentridge's new stop-motion film A Nicely Built City (Never Resists Destruction), the twelfth installment in his long-running Drawings for Projection cycle — the animated-charcoal film series that has anchored his practice since 1989. Alongside the film, the gallery presents a wide-ranging body of new drawings, sculptures and editioned works on paper tied to two of his current projects.

Kentridge's method, filming successive states of a single erased and redrawn charcoal sheet, has always made the act of destruction visible inside the act of construction, and a title like this one plays directly into that: a city nicely built is, in his hands, also a city perpetually being undone and rebuilt on camera. The new works extend the same visual vocabulary that has carried through his opera productions, theatre work and the sculptural glyphs seen elsewhere in the gallery's programme this year.

Coming right as Kentridge's survey "The Battle Between YES and NO" wraps up at Kunsthalle Praha, this London opening functions as something of a victory lap for an artist having an unusually visible year across institutions — making it a good moment to catch a global film premiere in a gallery setting before it inevitably tours further.

shows.title: sous ultra-vide
shows.description:
Elise Nguyen Quoc paints on wood panel using a spare vocabulary of acrylic and ballpoint pen, and the single work released ahead of this show - a long, low-slung panel titled "Absolument pas" - gives a sense of her scale and touch: a wide horizontal field worked over with the obsessive, repetitive mark-making that ballpoint encourages, layered under passages of flat acrylic colour.

"sous ultra-vide" (French for "under vacuum-seal") suggests preservation and pressure in equal measure, and that tension between the hermetic and the fragile seems to be the show's territory. It's a compact, focused solo presentation at Herald St's original Bethnal Green space, worth catching for anyone tracking younger painters working through drawing's slower, more compulsive registers rather than the gestural.

shows.title: Candy for Crocodiles
shows.description:
Dutch painter Ralf Kokke works in chalk paint, a matte, powdery medium that gives his canvases a slightly ghostly, faded-mural quality even when the palette is bright. The one released image from this show, "Blues Tiger," suggests the tone: a big cat rendered in cool blues, part heraldic emblem and part dream image, floating free of any clear setting.

Kokke's past shows with the gallery have leaned into a twilight, communal atmosphere - loose gatherings of figures bathed in blue - and "Candy for Crocodiles" looks to continue that register, pairing seductive titles with a slightly unsettling undertow. It's a good opportunity to see a European painter whose handling of chalk paint has become something of a signature technique.

shows.title: Painting & Caption: Works from the 1980s and 90s
shows.description:
Since 1986, Bernard Piffaretti has painted only one kind of picture: a canvas split down a vertical axis into two halves that look, at first glance, identical. This show pulls together early examples of the method from the 1980s and 90s, letting you see the "duplication" device in its formative years, before four decades of refinement wore it into something closer to a signature than an experiment.

The joke and the seriousness of Piffaretti's project sit close together. Up close, the two halves of any canvas reveal themselves to be far from twins - the angle of a brushstroke, the number of drips, the exact weight of a colour all drift apart under scrutiny. Piffaretti has described the effect as clouding "the origin of the time of the work," collapsing the usual hierarchy between a first, spontaneous gesture and its supposedly lesser copy.

Seeing the 1980s and 90s paintings together, rather than the artist's more widely exhibited recent work, gives a rare chance to trace how mechanical a rule can be and still generate paintings this alive - proof that Piffaretti found nearly everything he needed in the constraint from the start.

shows.title: Cemetery of Martyrs
shows.description:
Dala Nasser has spent two years travelling through Lebanon, Palestine, Syria, Egypt, Jordan, the UK and the US, taking charcoal rubbings from the graves of writers, artists and journalists connected to Beirut's intellectual history - a technique called frottage, used here to turn Peer's gallery into a symbolic graveyard. The resulting installation is a canopy of dyed and marked fabric draped over a site-specific wooden structure: black and green mourning cloth worked with ash, crushed malachite and shells sits alongside cyanotype-treated fabric bearing names, in Arabic, of those whose graves could not be found or visited.

Nasser is, at heart, a painter who has expanded the medium's basic materials - fabric, pigment, stretcher, mark - into large-scale, site-responsive works, and past projects have drawn on ancient sites across Lebanon and the wider region. This commission departs from that historical register to focus on more recent figures tied to the Nahda, the nineteenth and twentieth-century Arab cultural renaissance, framing artistic labour itself as a form of resistance and sovereignty.

Produced with Nottingham Contemporary and KM21 in The Hague, this is a major, research-heavy new commission from an artist who showed in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and the Aichi Triennale, and it's a strong reason to make the trip to Hoxton this autumn.

shows.title: Power of What (Memory Room)
shows.description:
Jyll Bradley turns Pi Artworks' new Shoreditch space into one of her "memory rooms" — an installation that folds together photography, sculpture and wallpaper of the artist's own design to recreate the psychic terrain of a specific place: the dilapidated greenhouse in her childhood garden in Kent where she set up her first studio in the 1980s. Solarised self-portraits from 1987, never previously exhibited, show Bradley turning away from the camera even as she seeks it out, an image of a young queer artist caught between visibility and concealment.

Around these photographs she builds sculptures in her signature material, plexiglass, here introducing a new dichroic surface that throws shifting rainbow colour across the room as viewers move through it. A major freestanding work first shown at The Box in Plymouth, Running and Returning, anchors the installation, harvesting daylight from the gallery's windows into its own spectrum. The effect is less a conventional exhibition than an environment for reflection, built from the vocabulary of light, agriculture and queer coming-of-age that Bradley has developed across three decades of practice.

This is Bradley's first UK solo show since her 2025 survey in Plymouth, and it inaugurates Pi Artworks' first full season at Perseverance Works after the gallery's move from Fitzrovia. Anyone who has followed her large-scale public commissions — the Hayward Gallery's The Hop, or Green/Light for the Folkestone Triennial — will find here a more intimate, interior counterpart to that public work: a room built entirely from memory.

shows.title: TIME TO SHINE! (the salesmen)
shows.description:
Hernan Bas turns his attention to the small, overlooked performances of retail life: the perfume counter attendant, the seaside seashell hawker, the gallerist who specializes in "cat-made painting." His new paintings cast these minor characters as leading players in the theatre of commerce, each caught in the charged, fleeting moment of a sales pitch — the instant that exposes vulnerability behind a professional smile.

Several works trace back to the artist's own childhood memories of mall culture and roadside stands, filtered through Bas's signature lush, decorative palette and eye for camp theatricality. Even the art world gets pulled into the joke: one painting depicting "two artists, a dealer and a collector" turns out, on closer inspection, to upend who's really the artist in the room. Throughout, Bas plays with the discomfort of being simultaneously seller and sold-to, noticing the specific tragicomedy of professions — the perfume-counter spritzer, the mall Santa, the door-to-door type — that already feel like relics of a vanishing retail world.

This is a joint presentation: the same body of work opens concurrently at Perrotin in Tokyo, making this London outing one half of a two-city debut for the series. It's Bas's first show at Victoria Miro since events at Ca' Pesaro in Venice earlier this year, and continues his long-running interest in performance, self-reflexivity and the theatrical undertow of everyday transactions.

shows.title: Send in the Clowns
shows.description:
Khalif Tahir Thompson's first solo presentation at Victoria Miro since the gallery announced his representation builds vibrant, collaged domestic scenes out of his own family archive — photographs his grandmother kept in storage for sixteen years after her death before his sister could retrieve them from Florida. What began as a small set of paintings honoring his maternal lineage grew into a wider series about growing up Black in Brooklyn, spanning Y2K-era aesthetics, sibling relationships and half-remembered childhood incidents.

The paintings layer paper, fabric and improvised strings of letters and numbers into the picture plane, pushing against the illusion of flat surface the way a collage insists on its own physicality. The title borrows from Sondheim's 1973 ballad — a phrase for summoning comic relief when a situation turns chaotic — which Thompson uses as a lens for how humor gets deployed to mask vulnerability within a family history marked by loss as much as tenderness.

Thompson, who trained at Purchase College and Yale, has shown at institutions including the Gantt Center and was included in Victoria Miro's own group show The Stories We Tell last winter; this is his proper solo debut with the gallery, and his work already sits in museum collections from the Smithsonian's African American history museum to the Nelson-Atkins and the Rubell Museum.

shows.title: Ha Chong-Hyun
shows.description:
Ha Chong-Hyun's inaugural show with Lisson, and his first in London since 2020, surveys six decades of a practice built almost entirely around one radical technical idea: forcing dense oil paint through the reverse of coarse hemp canvas so that pressure and material resistance, rather than the brush, determine the final surface. Known as Conjunction, the method has occupied Ha since the early 1970s and remains central to his identity as one of the founding figures of Dansaekhwa, Korea's postwar monochrome painting movement.

The show also reaches back further, to woven and folded canvases from the late 1960s that pushed painting toward objecthood, and to works from the 1970s where Ha burned impasto surfaces or embedded barbed wire and coiled springs — direct responses to material scarcity and martial law under South Korea's military dictatorship. Later Post-Conjunction works extend the same push-through technique into new registers of color, scale and rhythm.

Timed to coincide with Ha's retrospective opening at the Asian Art Museum, San Francisco, this is a rare chance in London to see the full arc of a practice that turned a single physical gesture into a lifelong inquiry.

shows.title: Pulse, Pause, Repeat
shows.description:
Curated by art historian Marie Perennès, this show gathers paintings, drawings and sculpture from the final twelve years of Carmen Herrera's extraordinarily long life, framing that late work not as a coda but as the culmination of an eighty-year investigation into line, form and color. Herrera trained as an architect in 1930s Havana, moved to New York in 1939, and spent the early 1950s in Paris, where her painting shifted from lyrical abstraction toward the hard-edge geometry that would define her — though she wasn't widely recognized until her nineties.

Across four rooms, the exhibition moves from diagonal, chromatically driven compositions (the interlocked red-and-blue triangles of the two-part Untitled, 2016) through rectilinear grid paintings like Escalera al Cielo, into a room built around line as a shape-making device, and finally into the black-and-white paintings Herrera began in 1950 as a way of stripping her color experiments down to their bones. Herrera's own description of the work — "two colours reacting or dancing with each other" — is a good guide to how precise and how playful these paintings actually are underneath their hard-edged calm.

The show precedes a major Herrera retrospective opening at the Guggenheim Bilbao in 2027, making this an early, more intimate look at an artist whose reputation is still catching up to the work.

shows.title: Sight Line
shows.description:
Sarah Schlesinger's second solo show with Huxley-Parlour presents twelve small, tightly cropped panel paintings that strip the seascape down to its formal bones. Rather than horizon lines and panoramic vistas, Schlesinger offers close-up fragments of water and light — hazy oranges bleeding into inky blues and murky greens, with no clear light source to anchor the scene in a particular time of day.

That ambiguity is the point. Working at an intimate scale, Schlesinger builds compositions that hover between representation and geometric abstraction, using the language of landscape painting to investigate something closer to the psychology of looking — how partial information, obscured views and shifting perspective condition what we think we're seeing.

It's a quieter, more contemplative show than the gallery's group survey next door, and a good showcase for an artist whose reputation has been built on precisely this kind of controlled, slow-burn intensity.

shows.title: Cecilia Vicuña: Living Threads
shows.description:
This is the first major UK survey of Cecilia Vicuña, the Chilean poet, artist and activist whose six-decade practice moves fluidly between painting, textile, film, ritual and performance, refusing to sit still in any single medium. Vicuña came to London to study at the Slade in the early 1970s and went into self-exile after the 1973 coup against Allende — an experience of displacement that hardens into the political charge running through much of her work, including a dedicated display on Artists for Democracy, the solidarity organisation she co-founded in London with David Medalla, John Dugger and Guy Brett.

The exhibition's centerpiece is Quipu Menstrual, a suspended mass of unspun red and brown wool that reactivates the quipu — the knotted Andean recording system Vicuña has spent fifty years reinventing as sculpture. Alongside it are the precarios, small ephemeral assemblages of paper, feathers and found debris she began making in London in the 1960s (only one survives from that period; the rest exist only as documentation), plus paintings from her London years and works from her ongoing Palabrarmas series, which treats language itself as a kind of woven material. The show closes with the UK premiere of her newest large-scale installation, Ciudad Geométrica (2025).

It's a rare chance to see the through-line of an artist whose current recognition — biennials, museum retrospectives, a Golden Lion at Venice in 2022 — took decades to catch up with a practice that was always, in its own quiet way, insisting on ecological memory and indigenous knowledge systems long before those became fashionable curatorial concerns.

shows.title: This Must Be the Place: Artists for Whitechapel Gallery
shows.description:
To mark its 125th anniversary and raise funds for its future, Whitechapel Gallery has persuaded twenty-four international painters and their galleries to contribute new or recent work for a selling exhibition staged in the Assembly Room — the space that once housed the old Whitechapel Library. All the participants share a commitment to painting as an open-ended process rather than a fixed statement, working across figuration and abstraction with a shared appetite for slow, accumulated surfaces over quick images.

The roster ranges widely in generation and geography: Andrew Cranston's book-cover paintings sit alongside Lenz Geerk's psychologically charged portraits, Jake Grewal's dreamlike figures dissolving into landscape, and Shiwen's hybrid botanical-architectural compositions. Younger London-based painters like Simone Kennedy Doig and Remi Ajani appear next to internationally exhibited figures such as Nathanaëlle Herbelin and Giangiacomo Rossetti, giving the show the feel of a cross-section of painting's current moment rather than a single curatorial thesis.

Every work is for sale, with proceeds split between the gallery, the artists and their representing galleries — a practical model for institutional fundraising that doubles as a survey of some of the most interesting painters currently exhibiting internationally.

shows.title: I Can't Complain
shows.description:
Autumn Knight's first major UK presentation takes complaint itself as its subject — its pleasures, its frustrations, and the political work it does when it's not simply dismissed as noise. Knight, whose interdisciplinary practice draws on theatre training, drama therapy and improvisation, transforms the ICA's Lower Galleries into a space built around a sound installation of recorded conversations in which participants air their everyday grievances, from the trivial to the structurally revealing.

The main gallery is dominated by a canopy of balloons, a recurring motif in Knight's work, framing the architecture around the sound piece; a selection of earlier video works in the back gallery trace her ongoing investigation into complaint as a social and performative act, involving objects and participants prompted to share their own irritations. Live performances punctuate the run — Knight performs solo on three dates in October, and later collaborates with London artist Samra Mayanja and the Brussels duo Michelangelo Miccolis and nick von kleist.

Knight has shown at major institutions including MCA Chicago, the Whitney Biennial and Performance Space New York, and her work WALL entered the permanent collection of the Studio Museum in Harlem — the first live performance piece to do so. This ICA show, humorous and uncomfortable in roughly equal measure, is a welcome introduction of that practice to London audiences.

venue.name: Institute of Contemporary Arts
venue.address: The Mall, St. James's, London SW1Y 5AH

shows.title: Cindy Sherman
shows.description:
Cindy Sherman debuts a new body of photographic work, Fabric Matrons, that pushes her decades-long interrogation of constructed identity into new, more dissolving territory. Where her earlier characters were often sharply legible types, the figures here are draped and half-swallowed by elaborate fabric, blurring the line between a person and her surroundings — a way of picturing how women negotiate visibility (or its withdrawal) across different life stages.

Many of the fabrics and accessories are drawn from Chanel's archives, extending a dialogue with the fashion house that goes back to Sherman's Ominous Landscapes series of the early 2010s. But this new work leans harder into theatrical styling and editorial photography's visual codes, only to deliberately sabotage their glamour with artifice that's a little too visible, staging that's a little too strange.

It's classic late Sherman: a body of work that uses fashion's own tools against it, turning the language of the photoshoot into a meditation on aging, performance and the sheer physical labor of maintaining an image over a lifetime.

shows.title: Previous & Ongoing
shows.description:
Lorna Simpson's first UK exhibition in eight years brings together paintings, collages and sculpture to show how thoroughly these strands of her practice now feed each other. Simpson made her name in the 1990s with conceptual photography that paired staged images with fragmented text; since turning to painting in earnest around 2014, she's built an equally distinctive body of large-scale and multi-panel works anchored in appropriated archival photography, much of it sourced from vintage Ebony magazine.

Treating found news and lifestyle imagery as a kind of sedimentary material, Simpson reconfigures and repaints these fragments so that history keeps accruing new meaning rather than settling into a fixed record. The show follows her first dedicated painting survey at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2025 and a major solo presentation at Punta della Dogana in Venice — the most significant showing of her work in Europe in over a decade, on view through November 2026 — making this London exhibition a chance to see how the paintings hold up outside the context of a museum retrospective.

Given how rarely her work has been shown in the UK, this is a significant opportunity to see Simpson's recent output — where photography, painting and sculpture are treated as continuous rather than separate practices — in person.

shows.title: My Blue Period
shows.description:
Romuald Hazoumè returns to the mask form that made his name — the masques bidons, faces built from repurposed plastic jerry cans and other found containers — for a new series timed to coincide with 1-54 and Frieze London. Where his earlier masks ranged across colours and materials, this group is dominated by blue, a choice that nods openly to Picasso's Blue Period and, at the same time, to the blues as a Black musical tradition born of hardship and endurance.

Each mask is titled after a person or place, and the works function as pointed, satirical portraits of specific geopolitical flashpoints — from resource conflict in the Congo to the war in Gaza and the war in Ukraine. Hazoumè builds these characters out of scavenged junk, adorning the containers with found materials so that each "face" carries its own history of use and discard, in keeping with his long-standing interest in consumption, waste, and postcolonial economies.

It's typical of Hazoumè's method: witty, materially inventive, and unsparing in what it has to say about power. Coming in the middle of London's autumn fair season, the show is a compact but pointed survey of where his mask-making has landed after several decades of the same central gesture.

shows.title: Amar Kanwar
shows.description:
Amar Kanwar has spent three decades making lyrical, essayistic films that sit somewhere between documentary and poetry, and this survey brings together a trilogy of major works to transform Serpentine North into a darkened, immersive sound-and-image environment. At its center is the feature-length Such a Morning (2017), shown alongside the multi-screen installation The Peacock's Graveyard (2023) and a new seven-screen work, The Charcoal Man, premiering here.

Kanwar's work returns again and again to the aftermath of the 1947 Partition of British India and the long, unresolved legacies of decolonization across the subcontinent — displacement, state violence, memory, and the quiet persistence of ordinary life under all of it. Rather than straightforward reportage, his films work through repetition, image, and voiceover to build something closer to visual essay or elegy, using specific histories to open onto larger questions about justice and power.

This is Kanwar's first major UK institutional survey in some years, and the chance to see three large-scale video works in dialogue — including a world premiere — makes it one of the more substantial moving-image exhibitions on in London this autumn.

shows.title: Change Ringing
shows.description:
Justin Caguiat's first major UK exhibition turns Serpentine South into a responsive, slowly shifting environment built around the gallery's own architecture. Centerpiece is a series of new thermochromic paintings whose heat-sensitive pigments continuously reveal and conceal different forms as the room's temperature and light change, so the work is never quite fixed — visitors on different days, or even at different times of day, will see different paintings.

Running alongside the paintings is a set of bronze bells, cast in the shapes of flowers and seeds, that chime in continually shifting sequences based on English "change ringing" — a bell-ringing tradition built on mathematical permutation rather than melody. The score, composed by Lily Pickett, uses the gallery's walls to gather and amplify the sound, turning the whole space into something closer to an instrument than a picture gallery.

Caguiat, who works across painting, sculpture, and site-specific installation, extends ideas from his recent Zodiac Machine project in Madrid — itself inspired by a self-taught architect's decades-long, materially improvised cathedral — into a meditation on how buildings absorb ritual and memory over time. It's an ambitious, sensorially rich show that treats architecture itself as a living material.

shows.title: The Debtor's Portal
shows.description:
Bahar Noorizadeh's first major UK presentation centers on two linked works that treat global finance as a kind of speculative fiction machine. The main piece, Free to Choose (2023), is billed as a "financial science-fiction opera" set in a future Hong Kong, made with Waste Paper Opera and Rudá Babau and loosely extrapolated from Yanis Varoufakis's popular explainer on capitalism — reimagining the credit-banking system as a delirious time-travel apparatus. Alongside it, The Space of Flows (2021) spatializes a scene from that same fictional universe: a 3D-printed car, imploded mid-time-travel, with video projected across its wreckage.

Noorizadeh's recurring motif is the car as an avatar for shifting economic regimes — Fordism, post-Fordism, and what she calls "Teslaism" or "Muskism" — using genre tropes from science fiction and gaming culture to make abstract financial systems legible as spectacle and myth. It's a practice that sits at the intersection of art, economic theory and world-building, closer to speculative design or game design than traditional video art.

Originally produced by Cooper Gallery in Dundee and reworked for The Showroom's space, the exhibition runs alongside a new exterior mural commission by the same artist, making this her most substantial UK outing to date. Recommended for anyone interested in how contemporary artists are trying to visualize the otherwise invisible machinery of global finance.

shows.title: That Which Appears
shows.artist: Olivia Bax, James Fisher, Lucy Gunning, Charles Hewlings, Milly Peck, Mike Silva, with works from the Drawing Matter collection
shows.description:
Co-curated by two of its participants, sculptor Olivia Bax and painter James Fisher, this group show takes the window as a shared motif across sculpture, painting, film and architectural drawing. Alongside new and existing work by Bax, Fisher, Lucy Gunning, Charles Hewlings, Milly Peck and Mike Silva, the gallery brings in historic architectural drawings from the Drawing Matter collection by figures including Louis Kahn, Mies van der Rohe and Christo, setting contemporary studio practice in dialogue with drawings originally made to plan real buildings.

The premise is simple but rich: a window is never just glass and frame, it's a hinge between inside and outside, a way of picturing memory, distance and threshold. Bax's playful, patched-together sculptural objects (assembled from polystyrene, plaster, net and household paint) sit at one end of that spectrum, treating the window as a lumpy, handmade object rather than a clean architectural feature, while the Drawing Matter works bring in the discipline's more rational, plan-based way of thinking about openings in a wall.

This is the first part of a two-venue project, with an expanded version due to travel to the Millennium Gallery in Sheffield in 2028, so London audiences get an early, more intimate look at how the show's central idea plays out before it grows into a larger survey with an accompanying publication.

shows.title: Imogen Stidworthy
shows.description:
Imogen Stidworthy's new installation grows out of three years spent filming and taking part in Primary Work, a therapeutic group practice developed by the Swedish practitioner Iris Johansson, whose own autistic perception shaped a method for communicating outside conventional therapeutic or neurotypical frameworks. It's the second half of a two-part project that began at Chapter, Cardiff, in spring 2026.

Built structures, sound, video projections and sculptural forms divide the gallery into distinct but porous zones, with a spatialised soundtrack transmitted partly through burn-out bronze casts so visitors feel it in the body as much as hear it. The work stays close to raw material — cries, words, bodies in motion — while gesturing at something harder to name: the shifts of energy and connection that pass between people in a group without ever quite becoming language.

Alongside the installation, a set of audio guides made by participating artists (developed through Matt's Gallery's Radical Audio Guides project) offer alternative, often non-verbal ways into the work — a fitting extension of an exhibition that is, at its core, about the many forms communication can take when words aren't the primary channel.

shows.title: Doorway Guardians
shows.description:
Three large woodcarvings by Annie Whiles have spent the past year rotating between the entrance spaces of Matt's Gallery, KARST in Plymouth, and Flatland Projects in Bexhill-on-Sea — a touring collaboration that treats the foyer, not the main gallery, as the site of the work. Doorway Guardians combines the visual language of British seaside kitsch with the carved, painted forms of medieval sacred sculpture, filtered through Whiles' memories of molded-plastic charity collection boxes from the 1960s and '70s.

Standing between 150 and 185cm tall and weighing up to 250kg, the figures are built to be touched rather than roped off — designed, in the artist's words, to be "preoccupied but open," gathering patina from visitors as they move between venues over the course of the year. There's a deadpan, slightly eerie humor to them: technically accomplished carving used in service of found-object charm rather than reverence.

This final chapter finds the Guardians installed in Matt's Gallery's foyer alongside Imogen Stidworthy's concurrent solo show in the main space — a fitting pairing of a project about public thresholds with one about the thresholds of communication itself.

shows.title: Lucie Rie / Hans Coper: Life at the Wheel
shows.description:
The first major show in almost three decades to put Lucie Rie and Hans Coper's ceramics side by side, drawing together more than 200 pieces from private collections that are rarely accessible to the public. The arc runs from Rie's earliest surviving work in 1930s Vienna through to the pots she threw in 1990, the year she stopped working, alongside Coper's first tentative experiments with clay — a material Rie introduced him to at her Albion Mews studio — up to the refined, architectural forms he was making shortly before his death in 1981.

Both artists arrived in Britain as émigrés and pushed back against the earthy, Bernard Leach-dominated studio-pottery orthodoxy of the time, developing instead a shared, austere modernism that still reads as strikingly contemporary. The twelve years they spent working together at Albion Mews forged a friendship that outlasted Coper's move to his own studio in Digswell and his later return to London before settling in Frome.

Spread across four rooms of a historic Mayfair townhouse that once housed the William Morris & Co. showroom, the exhibition is accompanied by a new hardback catalogue with essays by Tanya Harrod, Nigel Wood, Edmund de Waal and others — scholarly ballast for what is otherwise a rare chance to see two of Britain's most important postwar ceramicists in genuine dialogue.

shows.title: Different Faces
shows.dates_note: Studio Voltaire's page gives only an opening preview date, "Tuesday 14 July 2026, 6–9 pm"; no closing date is published.
shows.description:
At 89, York-based artist Christine Hazell has become an unlikely late-blooming portraitist, and this show — her first institutional exhibition — is a joyful, slightly uncanny document of that new practice. Working daily in coloured pencil from family photographs, snapshots and found images, Hazell reimagines faces belonging to friends, neighbours, artists and even the odd celebrity, exaggerating a jawline here or turning a curl of hair into pure pattern there. Each drawing at Studio Voltaire is displayed in a recycled vintage frame sourced in Yorkshire, hung directly above the source photograph it reworks, so visitors can trace exactly how Hazell's eye and hand transform a likeness.

The sitters have a particular resonance for this gallery: many are artists and figures from Studio Voltaire's own community across three decades, including Nairy Baghramian, Jeremy Deller and the gallery's director Joe Scotland, curated here by Hazell's children, Matthew Higgs (director of White Columns, New York) and architect Gaby Higgs. What began as a pastime encouraged by her family — partly to help with memory loss — turned into a prolific daily habit, with Hazell completing over 200 drawings in her first six months of practice.

There's real charm in seeing an artist arrive at a personal visual language so late and so suddenly, without the self-consciousness that usually accompanies gallery-ready work. The show doubles as an oblique group portrait of the London art world Hazell's son has moved through for years, refracted through an outsider's untrained, exuberant line.

shows.title: Forever and a Day
shows.description:
This is Thiang Uk's first solo show in the UK, and it arrives with a genuinely unusual backstory: the painter was born in Hakha, Myanmar, and fled political violence with his family as a child before settling in the United States, eventually training at Hunter College, MICA and Skowhegan. That layered history of displacement runs under the surface of paintings that read, at first glance, as pure abstraction — layered colour fields, radiating bursts of light, and forms that dissolve into one another across horizonless, mythic terrain.

Uk has described his shape-shifting compositions as pulling equally from the animist stories told by his grandmother and the Christian narratives of his childhood, treating formal invention and lived history as inseparable. Rather than illustrating a specific narrative of migration, the paintings aim for something more atmospheric: the sensation of holding more than one place, language and belief system in the body at once.

Coming off a run of well-received gallery and museum group shows in the US, this solo debut is a good opportunity to see a distinctive, luminous painterly voice before wider UK attention catches up.

shows.title: The Heroes 1965–66
shows.description:
This is the first UK exhibition devoted exclusively to Georg Baselitz's breakthrough "Hero" (Helden) paintings, a body of work made over a single, ferociously productive year between 1965 and 1966 when the artist was just 27. Loans arrive from Tate, Berlinische Galerie, Museum Frieder Burda and Museum Küppersmühle alongside the artist's own family holdings, assembling roughly a cross-section of the some sixty paintings, 130 drawings and 38 prints Baselitz produced during this period.

The paintings' central figure — a lone, oversized man standing or slumped in a ravaged, ambiguous landscape, dressed in torn military rags or nothing at all — was Baselitz's answer to the optimism of West Germany's postwar "economic miracle." These aren't heroes swinging fists in triumph; as the artist put it, he wanted them to look "broken, destroyed, ragged, tattered." Working just after a residency at Villa Romana in Florence, Baselitz drew on the distorted, excessive figuration of Mannerist printmakers like Pontormo, folding those inherited forms into a bruised, deliberately anachronistic answer to both Socialist Realism and the reigning avant-gardes of Pop and Minimalism.

For anyone who knows Baselitz mainly through his upside-down canvases of the 1970s onward, this is a chance to see the raw, figuratively unstable work that got him there — including pieces that anticipate the "Fraktur" paintings, where hero-figures are sliced and reassembled, a formal rupture that prefigures the inversions to come.

shows.title: A Dream That Rhymed With Mine
shows.description:
Hayal Pozanti's second UK solo show (and third with the gallery) brings together a year's worth of new paintings and works on paper built from her signature vocabulary of biomorphic abstraction. Working oil stick and oil pastel directly onto linen and blending pigment by hand, Pozanti conjures forms that hover between flower, body and current — never settling into a single identity, always mid-transformation.

The paintings on view move between two registers: a group of "vessel" works where a single anchoring form (a dark red vase, for instance, in The Endless Whisper of Their Warm Bodies) holds a moment of stillness against a swirl of colour, and unanchored, all-over compositions like All That Shines Outside of Itself, where blooms in cream, red and lilac dissolve into ribbons of turquoise light. Pozanti has spoken about small, everyday details — a mountain, a bodega flower — carrying equivalent spiritual weight in her work, treating both as points where the ordinary and the sacred meet.

It's an exhibition about noticing — about a synesthetic, almost devotional attention to the natural world's connective tissue, rendered in a hot, confident palette that owes something to Surrealism's dream logic without ever settling into pastiche.

shows.title: The Early Years, 1950–1968
shows.description:
This is a formative-years survey of Ibrahim El-Salahi, tracing the two decades in which the Sudanese painter forged the visual language that would later make him a defining figure of African modernism. The works on view — including Night Scene (1955), The Martyr (1958), and two untitled paintings from the early 1960s — predate the calligraphic abstraction El-Salahi is best known for today, showing an artist still working through European academic training (he studied at the Slade in London) against the pull of Sudanese subject matter and, increasingly, Arabic script.

The period covered, 1950 to 1968, spans El-Salahi's return to Khartoum from London, his early experiments fusing Islamic calligraphy with Western modernist form, and the political tumult of a newly independent Sudan reflected in a work like The Martyr. Seen alongside Vigo's concurrent Calligraphic Forms exhibition at Mason's Yard, this show fills in the earlier chapters of a practice most audiences encounter only in its mature, fully calligraphic form — valuable context for an artist whose 2013 Tate Modern retrospective made him the first African-born artist to receive one.

shows.title: North and True North
shows.description:
Firenze Lai's first UK exhibition, timed to Frieze London, is also her inaugural show since joining White Cube in 2025 — and it's a debut built entirely on new ground, with a body of paintings made in her London studio over the past year rather than work imported from her established Hong Kong practice. Lai has built a reputation on quietly unsettling figuration: compressed, slightly warped bodies caught in ambiguous social or bureaucratic postures, rendered in a muted, chalky palette that owes something to both comic-strip economy and the tension of Hong Kong's dense urban life.

The show's title, North and True North, gestures at navigation and orientation — themes that take on a different charge given Lai is painting London for the first time, working through a new city's textures and social choreographies with the same wary, observational eye she's brought to Hong Kong for over a decade. Expect the same compressed, almost cartoonish figures, now filtered through unfamiliar surroundings.

Lai has shown at the Venice Biennale and had a major survey at Tai Kwun Contemporary in Hong Kong; this exhibition is worth catching as an early look at how her practice adapts to a new geography.
